speaker: johncaulfield
text: Thank you, Mayor, and good evening, council. I'd like to give some COVID-19 updates. The first is you probably saw actually yesterday the governor moved on to what he has defined as a safe state Washington, which is a phased reopening of our state and of our economy. We're currently in phase one. It's a four-phased approach. However, Pierce County leadership, including the Pierce County Executive, Pierce County Council in Tacoma, Pierce County Health Department are looking to put together the information to request the state to allow Pierce County as a whole to move to phase two. Ultimately, that decision will be made by the Washington State Department of Health. Also understand that once phase two goes into place, there's a minimum three-week wait before a county can apply or move into phase three and then subsequently phase four after that, which would be the full opening of the county based on how things were in early March. Also late last week, the governor and the Four Corners State Legislature leadership came to an agreement to continue the changes, the temporary changes to the OPMA to allow legislative bodies such as yourself to continue to meet with virtual meetings. The other thing that they did is they removed the guidance language that the governor had included early on that legislative bodies were to only include things that were routine and necessary. So effective today, that is no longer a part of his guidance to elected bodies throughout Washington State. Also, we're hearing that this continuation, actually, it only goes through June 17th of this month, which is later this month. And what we're hearing from AWC is that it is unlikely that it will be continued beyond that, which means at your study session, which is scheduled for June 22nd, presuming that we're in phase two, it is likely that that would be an opportunity to have your first either full or partial city council meeting to be held in the city council chambers and have the chambers open for the public to attend. Of course, social distancing would need to be enforced at that meeting commensurate again with the governor's guidance and the proclamations that he's issued. So just wanted to give you a heads up on that. Last week, I had communicated that Pierce County is providing free personal protective equipment that's funded with federal monies that they have received from the CARES Act. They were supposed to provide that opportunity. Actually, here in Lakewood, we have been communicating with Pierce County as well as the Lakewood Chamber to undertake that process right here in the Lakewood Town Center tomorrow. However, that has been postponed. And so Pierce County DEM is looking to reschedule that here in the near future. Next item real brief, I'd just like to kind of give you a warning order in advance of hoping to have some more detailed information as part of your next regular meeting on June 15th, which is what the financial impact is to the city of Lakewood from COVID-19. What I can tell you is that, as it relates to the almost 19,000 cities, towns and villages throughout the United States, the estimated economic loss, revenue loss for the three-year period, 2020, 21 and 22 is projected to be $360 billion. For the city of Lakewood, for that same time period, it's currently estimated to be $12.1 million with most of it occurring in 2020 followed by 21 and then a smaller amount in 2022. However, based on some of our state shared revenues, including sales tax for half a month of March that came in late last week, that 12.1 million is probably gonna increase a little bit because the numbers in terms of what we have received just for sales tax, and again, only for half a month in terms of where the economy was shut down is a bit sobering. So we need to go back and sharpen the pencil to further detail and analyze what the impact could be for the rest of 2020, as well as we look into 2021. As you know, we have been working with our federal delegation to communicate not only what the impact is, but to express our support for some kind of assistance through an upcoming economic stimulus. Congress has actually passed several so far that has provided assistance, for example, to the business community and nonprofits, though nothing yet or actually has been done though nothing yet or actually in individuals through unemployment and things along those lines, though nothing yet for municipalities, whether it's a city, county, or even a state, though the states have received some monies as part of the CARES Act, if they had a population over 500,000, which most states do. So one of the things that we have been doing, quite frankly, is just holding off, waiting for the federal government to act. And, well, we have been assured, and certainly our delegation here in Washington State understands the predicament that we're in and is very, very supportive, and has gone on record supporting that local governments receive financial assistance to bridge this gap caused by this economic downturn that's caused by the pandemic. However, we can't wait any longer. You know, I'm concerned that the drawdown on our cash is gonna go a whole lot quicker in the next two to three or even four months. And while we ended 2019 in probably the strongest financial condition that the city has ended in probably a good number of years, certainly since I've been here, it's been improving incrementally over the years. That is still not enough, given the sobering impact to our general and actually our street fund as well. And I haven't even gotten into the potential impact to real estate excise tax, lodging tax, the loss of the TBD monies and things along those lines. So on June 15th, what we plan on presenting to you is not only what the revenue losses are going to be, but also a strategy on how we can, again, bridge that gap over the next two to three years if we do not receive any financial help from the federal government in the near future. And it needs to come soon, it really does. And if it doesn't come soon, there are gonna be significant cutbacks in services, even elimination of services across the board. But right now our approach is to utilize some of the one-time reserve monies that we have, because again, we ended 2019 in such a strong position over the next couple of years. Again, it's only one-time money. And then also, we've been very frugal since the beginning of March. We put in place a number of action strategies to essentially stop all non-essential and discretionary spending. So that has helped bridge the gap in the short term. But as we move to the next phase, the analysis will show what the impacts are gonna be on our services. And one of the exercise that our department directors are currently going through is identifying, okay, what does a 20% reduction look like in the general fund across all departments? Now, I don't think, or at least I'm hopeful we won't have to go that deep, but certainly having to go 15% is probably very realistic. Because again, our reserves are only gonna go too far compared to what the revenue loss is. I know this is not good news. However, it is the environment that we're currently in. We are gonna have to act quickly in the next month or so to be able to address this, to begin to make some changes. Again, otherwise, my concern is that in our general fund, we are gonna very, very quickly run out of cash and working capital. And we're not the only city facing this. Cities all over the country are already moving forward with cuts and things along those lines. So again, we'll have more detailed information as part of your June 15th meeting. And I'm hoping maybe I'll be able to get out to you well in advance of that, some of the work that we're currently doing. I thought quite frankly, we were there. And then last week we got the numbers that we got. And so we had to go back to the drawing board. So that's where we are financially. Again, more information to come on that. Some other updates, you might've seen a letter. Actually, I wanna thank our legal team, Heidi Wachner and Odgen Murphy-Wallace, the telecom experts down there, as well as Paul Busich and Shannon Kelly-Fong for Antiphody Spear for working on a letter, asking the FCC to provide more time regarding a particular ruling that they're looking at implementing regarding wireless sighting applications. And it's not just the city of Lakewood, but cities in general have concerns regarding the conditions of the sighting improvements, the concealment elements as well. The number of cabinets that can be out there for the things that are on these poles and towers and things like that. So we have asked for more time. We're not the only city that has done that, but again, we'll keep you appraised of how the FCC responds to this. And by the way, it's not just a local or Washington state issue. This is a national issue. At your next study session under reports by the city manager, the city attorney would like to give you an update on an interlocal agreement that we would like to propose to the council for review and consideration as part of your next regular meeting. And it's to form and for the city to sign on to be part of what's called the Pierce County Force Investigations Team, which is a team that's now required by law to essentially review investigations and investigation of certain uses of force such as officer involved shootings and things along those lines. And so this essentially formalizes that process. And again, the city attorney will have more information for you at the study session next week on that. I'd also like to report, actually, well, I'd like to pass on from Tiffany Spear, one of our planning managers. So her and Brian Humphries and human services, they have been serving points on working with the community in a census committee regarding the 2020 census. And actually given the circumstances, the census is moving along quite nicely here in Lakewood. Our returns are not as high as the state or even Pierce County. However, they are on par with national averages, approaching 61%. Also two of our neighborhoods with census tracts that in the past have had very, very low responses. For example, the Springbrook and Woodbrook census track in 2010, their response rate was 39.3%. Well, as of last week, they were at 47.3%. Still a ways to go to come up with the overall average, not just in Lakewood, but Washington State. That's a considerable improvement from just 10 years ago. Likewise, Springbrook was, their 2020 census response rate was 34.3%. And they're almost at 40% right now. And also the Census Bureau has extended the deadline to respond through October of this year. So we still have some more time. So we're gonna, our committee is gonna continue to work, particularly with those two communities, but also, or rather two neighborhoods, but also citywide to get people to respond to the census. But we're certainly headed in the right direction. And again, I think a positive trend, given again, the circumstances that are going on, since we can't get out there and knock on doors and things like that. Wanted to also let you know that last week, maybe week before, late the week before last, our Public Works Department did request to FEMA to withdraw our application for the LOMAR, which focuses on the floodplain in Springbrook. And so the reason for that is that was, FEMA was gonna ultimately, because of the outcome of that was gonna require us to identify a new floodway within that neighborhood. However, the reason for asking for the withdrawal is that really there's two issues. One is that there's an existing berm over by McCord Field along Clover Creek, as it enters the city, that is really kind of causing the problem. That in turn is creating problems going across I-5. And so before we get out ahead of ourselves and create a problem or create some issues where we're creating problems for that area over there, the Public Works Engineering Department would like to work with FEMA and particularly the state on those two issues before we come back and look at the LOMAR again. So the result of that will be that the floodplain and the floodways that were in effect in 2017, as determined by FEMA will remain, which is actually a good thing at this point in time. Earlier today, the Clover Park School District approached us and Ms. Grimley sent out an email to you asking if the council wanted to put a message in their upcoming newsletter, congratulating the class of 2020. And so we have drafted something for you. I know we sent that out to you. And if you have any feedback or comments on that, please let us know. And we'd like to know by close of business on this Wednesday, June 3rd. Likewise, I know I had mentioned last week that we had drafted an article for the city council as part of the upcoming Connections Magazine. And I know several of you have already provided feedback, so thank you. But if there are any others, if you have any additional feedback, please let us know. And so from one elected to another, or if there's some other way you'd like to handle, I'd be more than happy to help accommodate that.
